fields.title: Chatbot

fields.title: Handyman AI Assistant
fields.summary: Conversational LangChain agent that quotes handyman jobs, finds calendar availability, and books appointments through natural language.
fields.business_problem: Solo handymen lose hours bouncing between phone calls, a pricing spreadsheet, and Google Calendar to quote jobs and schedule them. Customers want instant answers, not a callback at 9am.
fields.tools_used: Python, LangChain, Google Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash), Google Sheets API, Google Calendar API, OAuth 2.0
fields.key_features:
- Pricing tool reads a Google Sheets price list and uses Gemini to produce a structured quote (price, urgency, complexity)
- Scheduling tool queries Calendar freebusy.query for open slots in morning/afternoon/evening windows
- Booking tool creates a Calendar event only after explicit customer confirmation
- Multi-turn conversational memory via LangChain
- Hardcoded America/Chicago timezone (single-region service)
fields.role_contribution: Sole developer — designed the agent loop, implemented the three tools, set up dual Google auth (service-account for Sheets, OAuth desktop client for Calendar).
fields.biggest_challenge: Keeping the agent from auto-booking before the customer confirmed a slot, plus handling Calendar's freebusy time-zone semantics correctly.
fields.what_learned: Agent quality lives in tool contracts — tight, typed, and idempotent inputs/outputs. Mutating tools (like calendar booking) need an explicit confirmation step in the prompt, not just trust.

fields.title: Campus SkillSwap 1
fields.summary: Student-to-student skill marketplace built spec-first with GitHub Spec Kit — pure Django 5 monolith with server-rendered templates.
fields.business_problem: Students want peer learning (tutoring, design, music) without paid platforms; the team needed a small but real product to test a spec-first AI development workflow.
fields.tools_used: Python, Django 5.2 LTS, SQLite, server-rendered templates, Bootstrap 5, GitHub Spec Kit
fields.key_features:
- 6 user stories authored as specs before any code (specs/001-campus-skillswap/)
- Auth (register, sign in, post a skill)
- Browse + search by case-insensitive title and category
- Booking lifecycle: request → owner accepts / declines
- Star-rating reviews (one per user per skill, replace-in-place)
- Owner-only edit/delete with 403 for non-owners
- Invariants enforced at form (clean()), view, and DB (CheckConstraint / UniqueConstraint)
fields.role_contribution: Sole developer — authored the spec, data model, and tasks before writing code; implemented all 6 user stories to match.
fields.biggest_challenge: Keeping invariants consistent across three layers (form, view, DB) without duplicating logic.
fields.what_learned: Spec-first AI development produces tighter code than free-form prompting; the spec catches edge cases the code would have shipped silently.

fields.title: Campus SkillSwap 2
fields.summary: Same Campus SkillSwap product re-implemented with Claude Code's research-plan-implement methodology on a Django REST + Next.js stack.
fields.business_problem: After building v1 spec-first, I rebuilt the same product on a separate stack to compare AI-driven development methodologies and architectures.
fields.tools_used: Django 5, Django REST Framework, Next.js 16 (App Router), Tailwind v4, React Hook Form, Zod, Cloudinary, PostgreSQL, Render, Claude Code
fields.key_features:
- Two-service architecture: DRF API + Next.js frontend with credentials: include session cookies
- Debounced search with shareable, bookmarkable URL state
- Image upload via Cloudinary (falls back to local disk in dev)
- Toast notifications via sonner
- One-click Render Blueprint deploy via render.yaml
- 15 e2e scenarios (e2e/scenarios.md) all passing
fields.role_contribution: Sole developer — designed the API, built the Next.js client, deployed both services to Render.
fields.biggest_challenge: Keeping session-cookie auth working across localhost:8000 (API) and localhost:3000 (Next.js) in dev, then translating that to the Render two-service deploy.
fields.what_learned: Research-plan-implement loops produce great per-file code but require disciplined re-planning when crossing service boundaries; without that, the API and frontend drift.
